extracted.intended_audience: stakeholders, industry groups, experts and members of the public invited to make submissions to the Productivity Commission and government policymakers
extracted.subtask_description: Call for submissions to the Australian Productivity Commission on 15 identified priority reform areas; submissions will inform the Commission's advice to government and be considered against fiscal constraints and other government priorities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Address one or more of the Productivity Commission's 15 priority reform areas
rubrics_metrics.description: The Productivity Commission has identified 15 priority reform areas for further exploration and will consult on these initiatives.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Submissions should engage with the Commission's identified priority areas. Examples of reform topics mentioned in the announcement include occupational licensing for electricians, abolishing non‑compete clauses, unlocking opportunities in AI and digital assets, streamlining regulation and the Single Front Door, strengthening the National Energy Market, leveraging health technology, and enabling prefabricated and modular housing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide information to inform the Commission's findings
rubrics_metrics.description: This is an initial call for submissions and the Productivity Commission expects its findings to be informed by the information collected through their consultation process.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Contributors should supply relevant evidence, data, practical examples and perspectives that will help the Commission analyse the priority areas. Submissions that clearly explain problems, impacts and potential solutions will be most useful.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be realistic about fiscal constraints and trade-offs
rubrics_metrics.description: The government will consider the Productivity Commission’s recommendations within the context of the fiscal constraints it inherited and will balance these against other government priorities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Submissions should acknowledge likely cost implications and trade‑offs, and where possible propose costed or fiscally realistic options or indicate funding/offset approaches to improve tractability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Propose implementable and practicable reforms
rubrics_metrics.description: The announcement notes 'we might not be able to run with everything, but we will consider all of it and see what we can progress.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recommendations that are actionable, clearly scoped, and come with implementation pathways (timelines, responsible agencies, regulatory changes required) will be more likely to be progressed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Focus on long‑run productivity and sustainable benefits
rubrics_metrics.description: The overarching objective is to address long‑run productivity challenges to boost wages and living standards sustainably into the future.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Submissions should articulate the expected long‑term productivity, wage and living‑standards outcomes, and where possible provide evidence or modelling showing sustainable impacts rather than short‑term gains only.

rubrics_metrics.name: Align proposals with existing government reform agenda where appropriate
rubrics_metrics.description: The government describes an existing ambitious productivity agenda (e.g., removing nuisance tariffs, streamlining approvals, competition law changes, National Productivity Fund) that reforms should build on.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Submissions that demonstrate how proposals complement or build on recent and ongoing government reforms (skills, education, energy, competition, infrastructure, health technology) may be more persuasive; indicate overlaps or synergies with existing programs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognise the multi‑term and multi‑decade nature of productivity reform
rubrics_metrics.description: The announcement recognises that turning around productivity will take longer than two terms and is a problem built up over decades.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Contributors should frame reforms with an appreciation for phased, long‑term approaches and, where relevant, include short‑term milestones and long‑term strategies.
